drafts.title: The Atlantic Crossing: 2,700 Miles, Twenty Crew, One Freezer Plan
drafts.lede: Twenty crew, 2,700 miles, three weeks without a shop and a galley that pitches: the crossing is cooked at the dock — the freezer by week, the one-pot rough-weather meals, the bake that lifts morale.

drafts.title: Two Eggs, Two Temperatures: The Yolk Sets Before the White Firms
drafts.lede: A firm poached white needs ~80°C; a custard yolk locks at ~63°C — so no single bath does both. The protein chemistry and the make-ahead poach-shock-hold-reheat line that plates a hundred eggs.

drafts.title: Cocoa at $6,700 a Tonne, El Niño Ahead: Buy the Winter's Couverture Before 1 October
drafts.lede: A Signal Fire on cocoa: futures fell about 60% from their 2024 peak, but disease (swollen shoot in 41% of surveyed Ivory Coast farms) and a warming West African belt have raised the floor for good. The read for the galley — buy dark couverture on the soft bean price, not the shelf price that never fell, and hold it right.

drafts.title: The Cutting-Board Verdict: Rubber for Raw, Maple for the Pass, and the Scar That Retires Both
drafts.lede: A galley equipment verdict on cutting boards: a 2023 study shows plastic boards shed up to 50 grams of microplastic a year, while a 1994 microbiology test found wood kills bacteria that survive on scarred plastic. The honest two-board system for a 4 m² galley.

drafts.title: Venice’s Ten-Day Window: Six Weeks to the Autumn Moeche, Thirty-Four to the Castraure Overlap
drafts.lede: The ten days when castraure and moeche overlap in the Venetian lagoon. The shortest seasonal window in European cooking — and what it demands of a yacht chef who happens to be in port.

drafts.title: elBulli: The Winter Closure That Made the Kitchen, and the 1,846 Dishes It Left Behind
drafts.lede: A June 1961 minigolf licence, a kitchen that shut five months a year because nobody came, and the 1,846-dish logbook that closure produced. The record behind the legend — the method it produced has a piece of its own.

drafts.title: Lime Only Slows the Enzyme That Greys Guacamole: Cold and a Seal Do the Rest
drafts.lede: At pH 4 avocado's browning enzyme is slowed, not switched off: one four-month kinetic study on avocado purée, and the lime, the seal and the cold that hold a galley bowl green.

drafts.title: San Marzano: The Sauce Tomato Grown to Be Tinned
drafts.lede: The seal names two plants and forty towns, the savour hides in the seeds you scoop out, and the tin beats the vine for lycopene by nearly four to one.

drafts.title: The Burger Grind: Three Cuts, Two Passes, Salt at the Pan
drafts.lede: Chuck, brisket and short rib at 2:1:1, ground twice from near-frozen and salted only at the pan: an open, tender grain no tub of mince can give — and the honest line on doneness.

drafts.title: What a Yacht Chef Earns in 2026: €4,500 to €14,000 a Month, and the 91-Hour Week Behind It
drafts.lede: Base by metre from three 2026 guides, graded for their bias; the package priced against the named rule; the tip clause that is not pay; and a six-line worksheet that ends in your number.

drafts.title: Weekly Brief, 28 August 2026: The Cold, Not the Bag
drafts.lede: First brief of the thread: the two calls still open on the board, the llampuga season that opened on Tuesday, and three cold-chain numbers that pass the brigade test.

drafts.title: The Lab: Does the Alcohol Cook Off
drafts.lede: The belief that wine and spirits burn away in the pan, put under a published test: the USDA retention study that measured what stays — from 85 per cent to 5 — by method and by minute.

drafts.title: Butter at Four Euros a Kilo: Fill the Freezer Before the Curve Turns
drafts.lede: EU butter was quoted at €398 per 100 kg in the week to 16 August — 45% under last year — and the first tick up is in. Cream is tightening and the futures curve has turned for the autumn. Four to six weeks to buy the season's butter and freeze it.

drafts.title: Palma: Trade-Only at Dawn, Everything Else Within Twenty Minutes
drafts.lede: Palma has its own wholesale market and fish auction and both are shut to a yacht by rule; the provisioning guide by how long you stay — the agent to call with hours, the merchants inside fifteen minutes of the Moll Vell with days, and the people who hold the cards with a week.

drafts.title: Provisioning Day: Twenty-Two Mouths, Seven Days, One Map
drafts.lede: The quay delivery lands in one go and the cold chain is measured in minutes; the protocol that gets a charter week's food from the pallet to the right shelf before anything warms — with the Station Map to pin above the fridges and an A5 card to print.

drafts.title: The Cheap Fish Go First: Sardine and Anchovy Before Bluefin
drafts.lede: The bet: through 2028 the cheap oily fish of the north-western Mediterranean get smaller and dearer while bluefin stays plentiful on a raised quota. Five named signals, the strongest case against, a falsifier you can read at the lonja, and the provisioning moves to make now.

drafts.title: The Ship's Cook Certificate: The Ten-Crew Line That Decides Whether You Are Legal
drafts.lede: Under MLC 2006 a yacht with a prescribed manning of ten or more must carry a trained and qualified cook — and the certificate that proves it depends on the flag, not the chef. The named rule, the three cases, where to train, what it pays, and the trap at the port-state inspection.

drafts.title: Sourdough Rewrites Wheat Fibre: The Acid Switches On the Grain's Own Enzymes
drafts.lede: A Brussels group followed wheat's arabinoxylan fibre through a sourdough ferment: as the dough acidifies, the grain's own xylanases cut the soluble fibre into smaller pieces. What that changes in a loaf, and what it does not prove about digestion.

drafts.title: Chamber or Edge: The Vacuum Sealer Verdict for a Galley
drafts.lede: Two Anova machines stand in for the two kinds of vacuum sealer; the physics that decides liquids, the FDA line that decides raw fish, and a counted study that says what a vacuum actually buys — with the verdict a galley can act on.

drafts.title: Bay Leaf: Better Dried, Never Frozen, Not Poison
drafts.lede: Nine leaves in ten are picked by hand from Turkish maquis and cross the border at three dollars a kilo. The leaf rewards drying, punishes the freezer, and was never the poison you were told.

drafts.title: Beurre Monté: Butter Turned Inside Out, and Why It Holds to 88 °C
drafts.lede: Butter breaks at 70 °C. Whisked into a spoon of water it holds to 88 — because you have turned its emulsion inside out. The mechanism on a primary paper, the numbers, the recovery ladder, and the emulsion drawn live.

drafts.title: Bouillabaisse: The Boil That Makes the Broth, and the Charter That Guards It
drafts.lede: The word is younger than the legend, the first recipe was a chef's, and the 1980 Charter is a promise between seventeen restaurants, not a law. The Marseille record, the hard-boil mechanism, and how to serve it honestly aboard.

drafts.title: Saffron: Threads Only, Sixty Degrees, and the Fraud Test
drafts.lede: Every thread on earth is a cutting of one sterile plant from Attica; nine in ten come from Iranian fields, and eleven in a hundred samples on European shelves were flagged in the EU's authenticity sweep. The dossier: what it is, how it works, and how not to be robbed.

drafts.title: The American Pancake and Waffle: One Whole-Grain Soak, Two Machines
drafts.lede: One overnight soak of whole grain and cultured dairy, then two different machines and two different jobs. The pancake is a sponge, the waffle is a plate, and the split happens twenty minutes before service.

drafts.title: The Waffle: Crisp Shell, Custard Middle
drafts.lede: Shatter-crisp shell, a middle close to custard, and an overnight batter that does most of the work while you sleep. The cue is the steam, not the timer.

drafts.title: The Source Standard: How Littoralicious Decides What Is True
drafts.lede: Every food-science claim you read here now has to clear a named bar. This is that bar: the journals, the labs, the tells that separate a real source from a plausible one — and the eight tests we run before a sentence about your body is allowed to print.

drafts.title: The Menu Agent: Turn Any AI Into a Superyacht Menu Designer
drafts.lede: A ~1,100-line prompt turns Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini into a superyacht menu designer: every menu anchored to a named touchstone, an automatic composition formula (two proteins, one starch, a garden that follows the vibe), a one-dish breakfast with a true fact, a self-improving palette memory, a non-overridable validation gate, and a one-page card you print from any browser.

drafts.title: Golden Onions: The Base of Everything
drafts.lede: A curry, a ragù or a soup can be flat with every other ingredient right — and the onions are almost always the reason. Here is why taking them all the way to gold before anything else is the most decisive twenty minutes in the dish, and how to do it properly.

drafts.title: What Your Nose Catches First
drafts.lede: Walk into a kitchen and your nose has already filed a report before you have looked at a single pan. It is not a general sensor but a triaged one — built to catch danger first and reward second. Here is what it catches first, why, and how a chef turns that order into an instrument.

drafts.title: Where Cooking Sets Its Direction
drafts.lede: Madrid Fusion, San Sebastian Gastronomika, MAD and the great food congresses — what each is really for, and which one to actually attend.

drafts.title: Natural Wine, Under the Microscope
drafts.lede: What natural wine actually is, what the science says about sulfites and faults, and how to read a bottle honestly.

drafts.title: The Tin, the Flake, and the Madeleine
drafts.lede: How canning, war, and migration built a childhood pantry the whole world shares — and the science of why those flavours never leave us.

drafts.title: The Machine Behind the Guides
drafts.lede: How Michelin, the World’s 50 Best and La Liste actually decide, who pays for the verdict, and which signal a working cook should trust.

drafts.title: Glutamate, Honestly: Cutting a Third of the Salt Without Losing the Savour
drafts.lede: Monosodium glutamate is about one-third the sodium of table salt, and umami makes a low-salt dish taste saltier. A Shore Larder profile of glutamate: the 1908 discovery, the honest evidence on sodium reduction and safety, and a two-item galley kit with a swap ratio for guests watching their salt.

drafts.title: The Capsule Is Not the Fish
drafts.lede: A two-year trial got high-dose DHA into the brain. The cognition did not follow. What one supplement paper leaves for a cook who feeds people fish.

drafts.title: Prawn Shells, Fermented Into Umami
drafts.lede: A 2026 Singapore study fed prawn by-products to six microbes. One mould turned shell-and-head waste into a glutamate load worth six grams of MSG per hundred.

drafts.title: The Green Purée: Holding the Colour
drafts.lede: A bright, spoon-coating green purée that stays green from pass to plate. The whole trick is a hard blanch, a hard chill, and never letting acid near it until the last second.

drafts.title: Your Palate Is a Personality Test, and the Science Is Half Right
drafts.lede: What food preference honestly predicts about personality — sensation-seeking and food-neophobia hold up; the viral claims (bitter=psychopathy, sweet=agreeable) failed replication. Includes The Palate Profile, a 12-question instrument scoring four axes into eight archetypes.

drafts.title: Cultivated Foie Gras Nears the Galley
drafts.lede: A duck liver grown from cells — no bird force-fed — cleared its first market in 2026. For a charter galley that plates foie gras by the kilo, the question is shifting from whether to which guest asks first.

drafts.title: The Preference Sheet: Reading the Document That Runs the Job
drafts.lede: A dislike is a preference; an intolerance is a safety brief. The sheet rarely tells you which — so you learn to read it like a chart, not a wish list.

drafts.title: The Sorrento Lemon
drafts.lede: A single oval lemon from terraced cliffs above the Tyrrhenian, its peel more than seventy per cent limonene — and why a yacht chef should buy it by name.

drafts.title: The Tuna Bloodline
drafts.lede: The dark stripe most cooks trim and bin is the most concentrated flavour on the fish. Treat it right and it becomes seasoning, not waste.

drafts.title: Two Jobs, One Salary: The Chef-Stew Hybrid, Decoded
drafts.lede: ’80 percent cook, 20 percent stew’ is not a splash of extra duties. It is two positions paid as one, and the rest-hours ceiling is where it breaks.

drafts.title: The 730-Plate Problem — A Working Method for Cooking for Crew
drafts.lede: A yacht chef serves 730 plates per crew member per year — same nine faces, no menu to hide behind. The mistake is to call it casual. The opportunity is touchstone-driven cooking: named real-world anchors, a weekly cadence built on Blue-Zone weekdays and ugly-delicious Fridays, and the nationality plates that make a crew member text their mother.

drafts.title: The Crew Pharmacy — Twelve Food Combinations Where the Pairing Does the Healing
drafts.lede: Twelve food combinations where the pairing does the healing — turmeric and black pepper for anti-inflammatory relief, tomato and olive oil for sun defense, tart cherry and walnut for sleep, ginger and mint for motion sickness. The crew cook as quiet medic, with one weekly rotation and a galley pharmacy drawer that fits in a bread tin.

drafts.title: Field Report — Ten Techniques From the Frontier Labs
drafts.lede: Ten techniques from the labs and restaurants writing the next decade of cooking — Noma Projects on fermentation stacks, Aponiente on marine biomass, Etxebarri on single-fire discipline, Spence and Blumenthal on sound as a flavour input, Alchemist on multisensory plating, Central on vertical ecosystem menus, Geranium and Tartine on point-of-use stone-milling, and Pic / Mirazur / Frantzén on Pacojet cryotextures. Each section: the lab, the move, the science, what it teaches, the galley translation.

drafts.title: Sous Vide Vegetables — The Bag You Open When Onshore Lunch Falls Through
drafts.lede: Eleven sous vide vegetable bags — built once a fortnight, held at −18°C for months, deployed in twenty-five minutes when onshore lunch is cancelled at 11:32. White asparagus in brown butter and parmigiano, artichoke barigoule, beetroot confit, and the Mediterranean rescue menu they assemble.

drafts.title: Inside the Test Kitchens — Twelve Food Labs Setting the Direction of Cooking
drafts.lede: Twelve food labs — Noma Projects, the elBulli Foundation, Mater Iniciativa at Central, Aponiente, Mugaritz, Alchemist, Modernist Cuisine, Pujol, Disfrutar, BCC Innovation, Atelier Crenn, Geranium — and what each one is currently working on. The R&D infrastructure of fine dining, surveyed for the working chef who wants to steal one transferable practice from each.

drafts.title: What Littoralicious Stands For — The Three Pillars, Written Down
drafts.lede: Three pillars, eight principles, one mission. The DNA of Littoralicious — the grandmother, the scientist, the yacht chef — written down so every article answers to the same standard. With the banned words, the voice rules, the design lock, the 11-PM test that every piece must pass before publication.

drafts.title: Thawing Fish Without the Drip: The Cold-Brine Method
drafts.lede: Air-thawing costs you colour and up to a third of the fish’s water. A cold salt bath thaws faster, holds the flesh red, and keeps the surface out of the danger zone.

drafts.title: Miso From Scratch: Koji, Salt, and Time
drafts.lede: Buy a paste and you buy someone else’s decisions. Build it from koji and you control the salt, the sweetness, and how much glutamate the mould sets free.

drafts.title: One Dial, Every Grain
drafts.lede: One setpoint for every grain: 100% steam, 100°C. Vary only the water ratio and the minutes. A grain-by-grain reference table, the science of one dial, and the par-cook-and-regenerate line for service.

drafts.title: Taking a Hard Shot Without Flinching
drafts.lede: The burn of a neat spirit is not flavour but a heat alarm ethanol resets to your own mouth temperature — and the cold, breath and one-swallow technique that switches it off, honest about where the evidence stops.

drafts.title: MSG, Honestly: Using Glutamate to Cut the Salt Without Losing the Flavour
drafts.lede: Few ingredients carry a worse reputation on weaker evidence than monosodium glutamate. It is the most-studied way to cut a dish's sodium without flattening it — and the science that condemned it never held up. Here is what glutamate actually is, the salt it saves on a long charter, and the one honest caveat worth keeping.

drafts.title: The Pairing Does the Healing
drafts.lede: A single ingredient rarely heals. The body absorbs most active compounds only as members of a team — and the cook decides whether the team turns up. This is the working chef's guide to the combinations that actually reach the blood, the ones that quietly cancel each other, the heat that…

drafts.title: How Many Senses You Have, and How Many Sit Down to Eat
drafts.lede: The "five senses" is a 2,300-year-old shorthand, not the instrument panel your guest is eating with. Here is the honest count, and the eight or more senses that actually build a plate of flavour.

drafts.title: The Smell of Cooking: Why Some Aromas Seduce, Others Turn, and None of Them Leave
drafts.lede: A pan of onions browning in fat is the most reliable seduction in any galley — and a sprout boiled five minutes too long is the fastest way to lose a saloon. Both are the same kind of event: trace molecules, detected at concentrations your kitchen scale could never weigh, read by a nose built to care. Here is the chemistry of cooking aroma — why the good smells pull, why the bad ones repel, and why neither leaves your curtains when you ask.

drafts.title: Eggs: What Every Dish Asks of Them
drafts.lede: When to stop whisking, when to salt, what heat does to the white before the yolk — the egg, decoded dish by dish.

drafts.title: Flavours That Stay in the Mouth
drafts.lede: Aged Comte, chorizo, Epoisses, vin jaune, absinthe — why some flavours sit in the mouth long after the bite, and how to build that persistence on purpose.

drafts.title: The Parting Gift: What Guests Take Home From the Galley
drafts.lede: What to send a guest home with - the small, edible, personal thing that outlasts the charter.

drafts.title: The Parmigiano Wheel: Tableside Theatre, Judged
drafts.lede: Parmigiano wheels, bamboo steamers, dushi boats, slate, salt blocks - the serving vessel is the first thing the guest tastes with their eyes.

drafts.title: The Preservative Paradox
drafts.lede: A 112,000-person study just linked eight common food preservatives — including added citric acid and ascorbic acid — to higher blood pressure and heart risk. What it means for a galley that runs on long-life provisioning, and what it doesn’t.

drafts.title: Whiplash: A Fermented Hot Sauce With a Sting
drafts.lede: A lacto-fermented hot sauce engineered for a clean, building heat - the one the crew steals from the galley.

drafts.title: The Sapiens Method: How elBulli Turned a Kitchen Into an Encyclopedia
drafts.lede: The method, not the foam: Ferran Adria's Sapiens loop — understand first, act later — and the five stages run against a real charter week. The history behind it is a separate piece; this one is the tool.

drafts.title: The Lab: Keeping Guacamole Green
drafts.lede: Press-cling, lime, a film of oil, the avocado stone — every galley has a trick to stop guacamole browning, and most are folklore. So a chef ran the test, side by side.

drafts.title: Cook the Port: Terroir as a Galley Workflow
drafts.lede: Most ports hand you one ingredient worth building the menu around. Cooking the place you are in — terroir as a workflow, not a romance — makes provisioning easier, the plate better, and the markup in Monaco optional.

drafts.title: Cooking for the Ozempic Guest
drafts.lede: More guests now board on a GLP-1 drug, and a rich tasting menu is exactly the wrong plan. The science of why appetite collapses on Ozempic — and the small, low-fat, protein-first service that keeps them comfortable, and fed.

drafts.title: The Equipment Verdict: What Survives a Season at Sea
drafts.lede: The galley runs on a handful of machines, and the fleet has hard opinions earned at sea. The gear that survives a season, the gear that dies on arrival day, and the one rule that keeps you cooking when a unit fails mid-charter.

drafts.title: Sourdough at Sea: The Science-First Loaf
drafts.lede: An open, blistered crumb and a deep mahogany crust — raised on a jar of flour and water you keep alive yourself. The wild loaf made reliable on a moving galley, where the acidity that flavours it also makes it keep. Interactive: scale it, tick it, cook it.

drafts.title: Sea Urchin: The Candy of the Sea
drafts.lede: Uni is a reproductive organ that tastes of sugar — and the reason why is two amino acids, glycine and alanine. The full profile: the candy chemistry, the alum trick that hides age, the four ways to use it, and how to keep something this perishable alive on charter.

drafts.title: Koji: The Mould That Cooks For You
drafts.lede: One microbe turns rice into sweetness, protein into umami, and a tough cut into something tender — before a flame is ever lit. Meet the fungus Japan made its national organism.

drafts.title: The One-Hour Lunch: Market Meals That Feel Special on Provisioning Day
drafts.lede: Provisioning day, one hour to plate lunch, a galley full of boxes. The move isn’t to cook faster — it’s to let the market do the prep and assemble with intention. Here’s the playbook.
